synopsis: RAND’s April 2016 Driving to Safety analysis estimated that demonstrating a fatality rate no worse than 1.09 per 100 million miles requires 275 million failure-free miles at 95% confidence; demonstrating a 20% improvement requires about 11 billion miles at 80% power [f6662, f6663]. The booklet treats this as a statistical reason for virtual testing: the rare-event logic transfers to off-road machines, but the numerical road-mile estimates do not, and the proposed approach combines simulation, statistics and targeted tests rather than relying on field hours [f15817, f15815, f15826]. However, Chapter 13 calls RAND 2016 an unverified research lead, creating a verification gap against the detailed claims elsewhere [f11203, f11275, f6662, f6663]. GAO’s reviews support knowledge before commitment: in its 2006 evidence, most of 23 major defense programmes began development with immature technologies, and 10 already expected more than 30% cost growth or at least a year’s delay [f9683, f9425, f9426]. A July 2026 GAO report covered 104 programmes; the chapter reports that almost half of middle-tier programmes entered with immature technologies, time frames were overly optimistic, and average capability delivery exceeded 12 years [f9523, f9427, f9428, f9429]. The booklet uses GAO’s principle for gate-based planning and ranges instead of dates, while explicitly warning that the supporting audit evidence is correlational and sometimes small-sample rather than causal [f15827, f9423, f16427].
